slides.kicker: PUBLIC LECTURE · HOW SHOULD WE LIVE?
slides.title: An Introduction to Ethics
slides.question: What makes an action right or wrong?
slides.sub: Results, duties, character, agreement and care: five ways to answer the oldest practical question
slides.notes:
In 399 BCE Socrates was sentenced to death by the city of Athens. His friends had arranged an escape. He refused. In Plato’s dialogue the Crito he explains why: he had lived under Athens’ laws all his life, and running away would break an agreement he had kept for seventy years. Whatever you think of his choice, notice what he was doing on the last day of his life: arguing about what is right, rather than doing what was easiest.
That is ethics. Not a list of rules handed down, but the attempt to give reasons for how we should act and live, reasons that others can test.
Next: what kind of question is an ethical question?

slides.title: Ethics asks what we ought to do, not what people actually do

cols.label: Descriptive
cols.title: What do people believe?
cols.text: Psychology and anthropology study which moral views people actually hold, and why.
cols.note: Example: most people would pull the lever

cols.label: Normative ethics
cols.title: What should we do?
cols.text: Offers and tests general theories of right action and good living: results, duties, character.

cols.label: Metaethics
cols.title: What is morality?
cols.text: Asks whether moral claims can be true, where they come from, and how we could know them.
cols.note: Example: is “you should” ever a fact?

slides.bottom: Surveys tell us what people think is right; ethics asks whether they’re right to think it.
slides.notes:
Three levels again. Descriptive ethics is the study of what people believe: surveys, cultures, evolution. That’s fascinating, but finding that most people believe something doesn’t show that it’s true. Normative ethics is the main event: theories of what makes acts right and lives good. And metaethics steps back further and asks what morality is. When you say torture is wrong, are you stating a fact, expressing a feeling, or reporting your culture’s rules?
Next: the map of tonight’s questions.

slides.title: Five big theories answer one question differently

rows.title: Consequentialism
rows.q: The best results for everyone affected

rows.title: Virtue ethics
rows.q: Acting as a good person would

rows.title: Contractualism
rows.q: Following rules no one could reasonably reject

rows.title: Care ethics
rows.q: Responding to the people who depend on us

slides.bottom: Most people mix these, but noticing which one you reach for first tells you a lot about yourself.
slides.notes:
Here are the five main families of answer. Most of us use all of them at different times: we think about results when planning a budget, about duties when keeping a promise, about character when we ask what a good friend would do. The theories try to say which of these is most basic, and what to do when they clash.
You can find out which one you lean towards in the ethics chapter of the Compass.
Next: the most famous way to make them clash.

slides.title: The trolley problem
slides.caption: A thought experiment
slides.text: A runaway tram will kill five people. You can pull a lever and send it onto a side track, where it will kill one. Most people say pull. Now imagine stopping it by pushing a large man off a footbridge into its path. Most people say no. Why, if the numbers are the same?
slides.notes:
Philippa Foot invented this case in 1967 to think about abortion and the difference between doing and allowing harm. Judith Jarvis Thomson added the footbridge. In surveys across many countries, around 80 to 90 per cent of people say you may switch, and a large majority say you may not push, even though both save five by killing one.
Each ethical theory has to explain that pattern, or explain it away. That makes the trolley problem a test for every theory we’ll meet.
Next: the theory that says only results matter.

slides.title: Consequentialism: the right act is the one with the best results
slides.sub: Everyone’s wellbeing counts, and counts equally

a.name: The case for
a.label: Bentham · Mill · Singer
a.lead: What could matter except how lives go?
points: Simple and impartial: no one’s suffering counts for more
Explains why lying and stealing are usually wrong: they harm
Demands real help for distant strangers
a.focus: Pull the lever: five lives outweigh one

b.name: The trouble
b.label: Williams · Rawls · Foot
b.lead: If only results matter, anything might be allowed:
points: A surgeon could kill one healthy patient for five organs
It ignores the separateness of persons
It leaves no room for integrity or personal projects
b.focus: Why not push the man too?

slides.bottom: Consequentialism is hard to resist in theory and hard to live with in practice.
slides.notes:
Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill argued that the right act is the one that produces the greatest happiness, counting everyone equally. Today Peter Singer draws the demanding conclusion: if you can prevent great suffering at small cost, you must.
The problem is that the theory seems to allow anything if the numbers come out right. A surgeon with five dying patients and one healthy visitor could quietly harvest his organs. Bernard Williams called this a failure to take seriously the fact that each person has only one life.
Consequentialists reply that a world where surgeons did that would be terrible, so a wise consequentialist wouldn’t. Whether that reply is enough is still debated.
Next: the theory that says some things are simply off limits.

slides.title: Deontology: some acts are wrong whatever the results
slides.sub: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785

challenge.title: Kant’s test
challenge.text: Act only on a rule you could will everyone to follow. Treat people never merely as means, always also as ends.

answer.title: What follows
answer.text: You may not lie, break promises or use one person to save others, because that treats them as a tool. This explains the footbridge: pushing the man uses him as a means. Switching the tram doesn’t aim at the one’s death.

open.title: Still unresolved
open.text: Kant said you may not lie even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding. And what if keeping a rule leads to catastrophe? Do absolute duties ever give way?

slides.bottom: Deontology protects individuals from being sacrificed, at the cost of sometimes letting disasters happen.
slides.notes:
Kant thought morality comes from reason itself, not from feelings or results. His test: could you will that everyone acted on your rule? A lying promise fails, because if everyone made lying promises, promises would mean nothing. His second formulation is more intuitive: never treat a person merely as a means.
This explains why most people won’t push the man off the bridge: you would be using his body as a tool.
But Kant famously said you may not lie even to a murderer at the door asking where your friend is. Many Kantians, like Christine Korsgaard, have tried to soften this. And most deontologists today, following W. D. Ross, think duties can conflict and must be weighed.
Next: a very different starting point, not acts but character.

slides.title: Virtue ethics: become the kind of person who acts well
slides.sub: Aristotle’s doctrine of the mean: each virtue lies between two vices
head: Too little
The virtue
Too much
slides.bottom: The mean isn’t ‘moderation in everything’: it is the right response, at the right time, to the right person.
slides.notes:
Aristotle didn’t start by asking which acts are right. He asked: what kind of person should I become? His answer: someone with the virtues, settled traits of character like courage, generosity and honesty, built up by practice, the way you become a musician by playing.
Each virtue sits between two vices. Courage lies between cowardice and recklessness. But the mean is not always the middle: sometimes the right amount of anger is a lot. It is whatever a practically wise person would feel and do in that situation.
For Aristotle, living virtuously is what flourishing, eudaimonia, consists in.
Next: the same idea, independently, in China.

slides.title: Character-based ethics appears across the world
slides.sub: Different traditions, a shared focus on who we become

items.caption: Mencius
items.text: Human nature has sprouts of goodness

items.caption: The Buddha
items.text: Compassion and the noble eightfold path

items.caption: Rosalind Hursthouse
items.text: Modern virtue ethics: right = what the virtuous would do

items.caption: Practice makes character
items.text: Virtues are learned like crafts, by doing

slides.bottom: Ask not only ‘what should I do?’ but ‘who am I becoming by doing it?’
slides.notes:
Character ethics isn’t only Greek. Confucius taught that a good person cultivates ren, humaneness, through ritual, learning and relationships. Mencius said every person is born with sprouts of goodness, like the instinct to rescue a child about to fall into a well, which must be nurtured like plants. Buddhist ethics trains compassion and wisdom through practice. In the twentieth century, philosophers like Elizabeth Anscombe and Rosalind Hursthouse revived virtue ethics in the West.
The common idea: ethics is less like following a rulebook and more like learning a skill.
Next: what if morality is an agreement?

slides.title: Morality may be what we could justify to each other, or how we care for each other
slides.sub: Two theories that start from relationships

cols.label: Contractualism
cols.title: Rules no one could reasonably reject
cols.text: T. M. Scanlon: an act is wrong if any principle allowing it could be reasonably rejected by someone affected. Morality is about being able to justify yourself face to face.
cols.note: Explains rights; struggles with animals and future people

cols.label: Care ethics
cols.title: Responding to need
cols.text: Carol Gilligan, Nel Noddings, Virginia Held: real moral life starts from relationships of dependence, such as parent and child or carer and patient, not from abstract strangers.
cols.note: Puts care work at the centre; risks favouring those close to us

slides.bottom: Both shift the question from ‘what maximises?’ to ‘what do we owe each other?’
slides.notes:
Contractualism, in Scanlon’s version, says morality is about what we could justify to each other. Could the one person on the side track reasonably reject a rule that lets you divert the tram? Perhaps not. Could the man on the bridge reasonably reject a rule that lets people push him? Surely yes.
Care ethics, developed by Carol Gilligan and Nel Noddings, criticised traditional theories for imagining morality as relations between independent, equal strangers. Most of life involves dependence: children, the sick, the old. A good theory should start there.
Next: the case that tests how far our duties to strangers go.

slides.title: The drowning child: distance may not matter morally
slides.sub: Peter Singer, Famine, Affluence, and Morality, 1972

challenge.title: The case
challenge.text: You walk past a shallow pond where a child is drowning. Wading in will ruin your expensive shoes. Must you save the child?

answer.title: Singer’s argument
answer.text: Of course you must. But the price of those shoes, given to an effective charity, can save a child far away. Distance and numbers of other bystanders don’t change your duty. So most of us should be giving much more than we do.

open.title: Objections
open.text: Is there a difference between rescue and ongoing aid? Can morality demand so much that it swallows your whole life? Do we have special duties to family and neighbours first?

slides.bottom: If you can prevent something very bad at small cost, many think you must, wherever the victim is.
slides.notes:
Peter Singer’s argument is short and hard to escape. If you can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, you ought to do it. Letting a child drown to save your shoes is monstrous. But a few hundred pounds given to an effective charity can save a life, and most of us spend that on things far less important.
Critics say morality cannot be that demanding, that we have special duties to those near us, or that charity is different from rescue. Each theory you’ve met gives a different answer.
Next: is any of this objectively true?

slides.title: Is morality objective, or something we make?

cols.label: Realism
cols.title: A fact, like maths
cols.text: Moral truths hold whatever anyone thinks (Plato, Parfit, Enoch).

cols.label: Constructivism
cols.title: The result of reasoning together
cols.text: True, but because reasonable agents would agree, not because it’s ‘out there’ (Kant, Korsgaard, Rawls).

cols.label: Expressivism
cols.title: An expression of attitude
cols.text: ‘Wrong!’ voices disapproval and commitment, not a description (Hume, Ayer, Blackburn).

cols.label: Error theory
cols.title: Always false
cols.text: Moral claims try to state facts, but there are none (Mackie). Not ‘anything goes’: just no moral facts.

slides.bottom: Even sceptics about moral facts usually still condemn cruelty: metaethics changes what condemning is, not whether we do it.
slides.notes:
When you say torturing for fun is wrong, are you stating a fact? Realists say yes: there are moral truths, as there are mathematical ones. Constructivists say moral truths are what reasonable people would agree to. Expressivists, following Hume, say moral talk expresses attitudes, a kind of booing and cheering refined into reasoning. J. L. Mackie’s error theory says moral claims aim at facts that don’t exist.
It’s important not to misread the sceptics: Mackie didn’t think torture is fine. He thought there’s no objective property of wrongness, and that we must invent our morality and stand by it.
Next: the whole field on one page.

slides.title: Every theory is strongest where the others are weakest
head: Theory
What it gets right
What it must answer
slides.bottom: Many philosophers end up pluralists, weighing results, duties and character case by case.
slides.notes:
Put the theories side by side and something striking appears: each one is strongest exactly where the others are weakest. That’s why many philosophers, following W. D. Ross, are pluralists: several things matter, and practical wisdom weighs them. Others think one theory can be refined to absorb the truths in the rest, as Derek Parfit argued in On What Matters.
Next: a toolkit for your own moral arguments.

slides.title: Four questions to test any moral claim

steps.title: Universalise
steps.text: Would it be all right if everyone did it?

steps.title: Count the effects
steps.text: Who is helped and harmed, and how much?

steps.title: Ask about character
steps.text: What would doing this make of you?

steps.title: Justify it face to face
steps.text: Could you explain it to the person most affected?

slides.bottom: When all four agree, you can be confident; when they clash, you’ve found the real moral question.
slides.notes:
Here is a practical toolkit drawn from the four theories. If everyone did it, would it work? What are the effects on everyone? What kind of person does it make you? Could you justify it to the person who loses most?
When all four agree, you can be fairly confident. When they disagree, you have found the genuinely hard question, and that is where moral thinking really starts.
Next: what ethics leaves us with.

slides.title: Ethics doesn’t give us a rulebook
slides.sub: It leaves us with better questions
questions: When may we sacrifice one to save many?
How much do we owe to strangers?
slides.line: The question is not just what to do, but what kind of person, and what kind of world, our choices create.
slides.notes: Ethics doesn’t give us a rulebook to follow without thinking. It gives us better questions and better ways to test our answers. The deepest of them may be Socrates’ own: how should one live?

slides.title: Discussion: bring the theory back to real life
questions: Should a self-driving car be programmed to sacrifice its passenger to save five pedestrians?
Is it wrong to eat meat if you could easily avoid it?
Should you report a friend who cheated in an exam?
slides.line: State your principle first, then test it against the other theories.
slides.notes: Three questions to argue about. For each, try answering as a consequentialist, a Kantian, a virtue ethicist and a care ethicist. Where do they agree? Where do they split? You can test your instincts on the trolley problem and its variants in the Trolley Gauntlet game.
